newsitem.title: FINLAND: Polls open in Finnish Euro-elections.
newsitem.headline: Polls open in Finnish Euro-elections.

text.p: Thick fog hung over the capital on Sunday morning as voters went to the polls in twinned European Parliament and municipal elections which may reveal a touch of Euro-scepticism among the Finns.

Polling booths are open from 0600-1700 GMT, when the initial results of advance voting in both polls -- by about one-fifth of eligible voters in the week ahead of polling day -- are due. No exit polls of significance are planned.
Unofficial results from the local vote are due around 1930 GMT, and from the European poll at 2000.

Party support remains little changed with backing for the pro-Europe government coalition partners unshaken, but personal support for the most visible opponent of the EU, and especially of a single European currency, has suddenly picked up.
Esko Seppanen, a vocal left-wing Euro-sceptic, has become the most popular individual candidate, backed by almost 11 percent of the electorate, opinion polls say.
Finland joined the European Union with Austria and Sweden in January 1995 after a referendum in which membership won 57 percent support, but this is the first direct poll for Euro MPs.
Voters will elect 16 representatives to the Strasbourg-based parliament from 207 candidates in nationwide balloting.
Each candidate has to be selected by their number, and leading daily Helsingin Sanomat carried a cartoon of a confused voter trying to make his choice based on shoe size.

Less than one-tenth of Finns have in recent surveys said they felt very negative about EU membership, with 71 percent finding EU membership favourable or neutral -- but about 60 percent are against a single currency.

Advance votes suggest the turnout could fall to as low as 50-60 percent against over 70 percent in a general election, and no-shows by apathetic voters could paint a more Eurosceptic picture than expected so far.

Few issues -- except Finland's adhesion last weekend to Europe's currency stability mechanism in the run-up to a single currency -- have featured in campaigning for the Euro-elections, which the press have dubbed "the celebrity poll".
An Oscar-winning filmmaker, a gay television weatherman, a popular singer and an Olympic gold-medal skier are running alongside political heavyweights.
Commentators say Social Democrat Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen's five-party coalition faces no serious upset.

His party recently saw its support boosted, and a survey for television news on Friday gave it 26.5 percent of the vote. The main opposition Centre Party, only ever half-heartedly anti-Europe, was a clear second with 22.5 percent.
